openers.organic-matter-humus-and-decomposition: Every year a forest drops a fresh cover of leaves, bark, needles and twigs onto its soil. This chapter follows that dead material as it rots. Decomposition breaks it into carbon dioxide, water, simple sugars and mineral salts, and releases its nutrients in forms that roots can take up again. Part of it escapes that fate and turns into a dark, stable substance that improves soil structure and holds nutrients until plants need them. Some of it breaks down within about ten years, while the most stable part resists decay for a century or more.

soil-bio-106.title: Plant litter, the fallen cover on the soil
soil-bio-106.text: Leaves make up about 70 percent of what a forest drops each year. Plant litter is all the dead plant material, such as leaves, bark, needles and twigs, that falls onto the soil surface. It forms the litter layer, the {{ref:soil-form-006}} at the top of many soils. Fresh litterfall is undecomposed, and its species and type are easy to recognize. Pieces over 2 cm in diameter count as coarse litter, smaller ones as fine litter. Soil scientists split the layer by decay: L for little decomposed, F for partly decomposed and H for fully decomposed and mostly unrecognizable. Grasslands, with little perennial tissue above ground, shed little litter. Litterfall also declines with latitude. Fast decay keeps tropical rainforest litter thin, while slow decay builds thick litter in boreal forests. The loose cover does real work. It shields aggregates from raindrop impact, so clay and silt do not plug the pores, and it helps rain soak in. It keeps soil moist, reduces erosion and shelters small animals. As it rots, litter becomes {{ref:soil-bio-112}} and releases nutrients. Most of the plant growth made on land, its net primary production, ends up eaten by herbivores or as litterfall. Litter therefore indicates how productive an ecosystem is and helps predict nutrient cycling and how fertile a soil will be. Fire can remove it completely, and regions with frequent wildfires have sparser vegetation and less litter.

soil-bio-114.title: Organic matter, the carbon left by living things
soil-bio-114.text: In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made {{ref:soil-fert-021}} in a laboratory, and an old idea began to crack. That idea, vitalism, equated organic with living. Organic matter is the large pool of carbon-based compounds derived from the feces and remains of plants, animals and other organisms. Its basic structures come from cellulose, tannin, cutin and {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, with proteins, lipids and carbohydrates. After an organism dies, microbes and fungi break it down. The small products can recombine into larger, complex molecules. Its molecules range from 200 to 20,000 amu, and up to one-third of its carbon sits in stable rings that are hard to break. In soil, litter decayed beyond recognition counts as {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Organic matter carries nutrients, holds water and buffers solutions towards neutral pH. Most measurements capture only organic carbon, so they only approximate the amount of once-living matter.

soil-bio-115.title: Decomposition, the breakdown that recycles the living world
soil-bio-115.text: Rotting plants release over 90 percent of the carbon dioxide given off each year. That rotting is decomposition: the breakdown of dead organic substances into simpler matter such as carbon dioxide, water, simple sugars and mineral salts. It recycles the finite matter of the biosphere. Chemical or physical forces drive abiotic decomposition. Living organisms, mostly microbes, drive biotic decomposition, also called biodegradation. Plant matter decays in stages. Water first leaches out the soluble carbon compounds. Soil invertebrates then fragment the litter, and microbes chemically alter what remains. In soil the reactions fall into three groups. Enzymes oxidize compounds to carbon dioxide, water and heat; nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur are released; and resistant compounds form that make up {{ref:soil-bio-089}}. The rate depends on temperature, moisture, soil properties, the amount and quality of dead material, and the microbes themselves. Decay is slow in very wet or very dry soil and fastest in damp soil with enough oxygen. When dry soil is rewetted, many bacterial cells burst and release a pulse of nutrients. Materials differ too. Sugars and amino acids are labile, quick to break down. Cellulose and hemicellulose are moderately labile. In a temperate climate their half-life is 12–18 days. {{ref:soil-bio-116}} and cutin resist, so resistant material builds up as soil organic matter ages. Acid and clay-rich soils decompose organic matter more slowly, because clay binds it out of microbes' reach. Turning the soil speeds decay by adding oxygen and exposing fresh organic matter.

soil-bio-089.title: Humus, the dark and stable end of decay
soil-bio-089.text: Humus usually makes up five percent or less of a soil's volume, yet soils lean on it heavily. Humus is the stable, well-decomposed form of soil organic matter, derived from the breakdown of plant and animal remains. The word is Latin for ground or earth. It is brown to black and made largely of carbon, with high amounts of nitrogen and smaller amounts of phosphorus and sulfur. Its {{ref:soil-fert-184}} commonly runs between 8:1 and 15:1, with a median of about 12:1. Only fully decomposed matter counts as humus. Material still decomposing is {{ref:soil-bio-112}}, and since the change is gradual, no sharp line divides them. Neither is truly dead, for bacteria, fungi and other microorganisms permeate both. Humus is amorphous, lacking the cellular structure of the organisms it came from. It occurs mostly in the upper soil. A humic layer of finely divided organic matter, with a large surface area, lies above the topsoil and below the leaf litter. Humus is an essential nutrient source and improves soil texture qualities. In sands and other coarse soils it holds moisture, and it lowers bulk density. Farmers also use the word for mature woodland {{ref:soil-fert-028}} spread to improve soil.

soil-bio-112.title: Detritus, where most of the land's food ends up
soil-bio-112.text: On land, far more material is broken down as dead matter than is ever eaten alive. That dead matter is detritus: the decomposing remains of organisms and plants, together with feces. On land it occurs as plant litter and as organic matter mixed into the soil, such as the humic soil beneath a layer of fallen leaves. In forests, leaf, twig and bacterial litter dominate it by biomass. It shelters seedlings, arthropods, reptiles and amphibians. Dead remains and feces gradually lose their form, worn down by physical processes and by grazers, bacteria and fungi. Communities of microorganisms usually colonize detritus and remineralise it, returning it to simple mineral forms. The organisms at work may be rot organisms, detritivores or coprophages, which eat dung. Late in decomposition, mesophilic microorganisms, which favor moderate temperatures, break down the residue and release heat. The same effect warms a heap of {{ref:soil-fert-028}}. As detritus decomposes on the ground, it feeds plants with inorganic salts. Water has its detritus too. In fresh water most of it is leaf litter from nearby land, the main carbon source of small streams. At sea it settles as marine snow of dead plankton and fecal pellets.

soil-bio-120.title: Mineralization, turning dead tissue back into plant food
soil-bio-120.text: Soil microbes face a nitrogen shortage. Most organic matter reaching soil holds too little nitrogen for the microbes that consume it. Mineralization is the decomposition, or oxidation, of organic compounds that releases their nutrients in soluble inorganic forms plants can take up. It raises the availability chiefly of nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur. Its opposite is {{ref:soil-fert-121}}, in which microbes lock nutrients into their own cells. Which process wins depends on a nutrient's concentration relative to the carbon in the organic matter. Above a carbon-to-nitrogen (C:N) ratio of about 30:1, microbes absorb mineral nitrogen from the soil and keep it away from plants. As they work, they release carbon dioxide, and the ratio falls. Below about 25:1, further decomposition releases inorganic nitrogen as ammonium. Nitrogen can end as ammonium, nitrite, nitrate or nitrogen gases. Carbon becomes carbon dioxide, carbonates and methane, and phosphorus becomes phosphate ions. When decomposition is complete, the freed nitrogen adds to the soil's total mineral nitrogen. The fraction that escapes mineralization goes the other way, into {{ref:soil-bio-090}}.

soil-bio-118.title: Particulate organic matter, the fast fuel of soil life
soil-bio-118.text: Pass soil through a fine sieve, and some organic matter stays behind. Particulate organic matter, or POM, is the fraction that does not pass a filter or sieve with openings usually between 0.053 millimeters (53 μm) and 2 millimeters. It still shows its original cellular structure: partly decomposed plant litter, animal feces, microbial detritus and pollen. Its carbon is particulate organic carbon, or POC, and there is typically about twice as much POM as POC. Most POM turns over in less than 10 years, though less active parts may take 15 to 100 years. Its decay supplies much of the energy of soil organisms and a steady release of nutrients. Fungal threads colonizing it bind particles with sticky polysaccharides into aggregates, improving infiltration, aeration and resistance to erosion. Manure and crop residues raise POM, while repeated working of the soil and turning native grassland into farmland deplete it. Because it responds quickly to management, it is often used as an indicator of soil quality.

soil-bio-090.title: Humification, how part of the litter becomes humus
soil-bio-090.text: Not all decaying matter vanishes into carbon dioxide. In humification, soil organisms feeding on litter turn part of it into humus instead of mineralizing it completely. The raw materials are plant detritus, dead animals and microbes, called necromass, the excreta of all soil organisms and black carbon from past fires. Fungi and bacteria that feed on dead matter do the work, along with earthworms, nematodes, protozoa and arthropods. Earthworms are major contributors. The ingredients disappear in order. Sugars, starches, simple proteins and organic acids go first and fast. Cellulose and {{ref:soil-bio-116}} follow more slowly, and fats, waxes and resins persist longest. {{ref:soil-bio-129}} transform that tough polymer quickly, making it a main precursor of humus. Resistant leftovers, such as modified lignins, oils, fats and waxes, join newly made compounds like polysaccharides to form the basis of humus. Reactions with proteins lock nitrogen and other nutrients inside, protecting them from mineralization. Early work pictured humification as building polymers that microbes could not attack. Recent research shows microbes can digest humic substances in redox reactions. Humification happens naturally in soil and artificially in {{ref:soil-fert-029}}, and it can darken soils, a change called melanization. For storing carbon long term, stimulating it beats slowing litter decay. Not everyone accepts the idea, though. Some authors reject humification as a distinct process, arguing that soil organic matter is a continuum of progressively decomposing compounds.

soil-bio-094.title: Why farmers prize humus
soil-bio-094.text: Weight for weight, humus holds nutrients many times better than clay. Its main gifts to farm soils are better structure and a large surface that holds nutrients until plants need them. Humus is a negatively charged colloid, and it raises a soil's cation-exchange capacity. Nutrient cations cling to it where roots can reach them instead of leaching away. On a dry-weight basis its cation and anion exchange capacity is many times that of clay colloids. Humus can hold the equivalent of 80–90% of its weight in moisture, helping soil withstand drought. It increases microporosity, and microbial mucilages secreted during humification glue particles into a crumbly, well-aerated tilth. It buffers soils against excess acidity or alkalinity. It also chelates, or chemically grips, heavy metals and excess nutrients, keeping them from leaching. Its dark color helps cold soils warm in spring. Whether roots absorb humic substances was long debated. The consensus now is that humus acts on plants hormonally, not simply as food.

soil-bio-093.title: Why some humus lasts centuries and some a decade
soil-bio-093.text: Much of the humus in soil today has persisted for more than 100 years. It survives because it hides inside small soil aggregates or binds tightly to clays, out of reach of microbes and their enzymes. Humus without that protection mostly decomposes within 10 years and is called labile. The two kinds do different jobs. Labile, or effective, humus is a ready nutrient supply for microbes. Stable humus offers plants few nutrients but helps maintain soil structure as a long-term reservoir. Its most stable forms, often called {{ref:soil-bio-105}}, may persist for centuries if not millennia. Earthworms, termites and some millipedes build mineral-organic complexes in their guts. Surface layers shaped by such animals therefore store more carbon than those where litter simply piles up. Charcoal powder mixed into topsoil slowly oxidizes into a very stable humus, probably important in creating the fertile Amazonian {{ref:soil-class-053}}. Only humus with multi-century permanence matters for drawing down excess carbon dioxide from the air. In subtropical and tropical climates, heat and heavy leaching oxidize litter and humus rapidly. Without new organic inputs, humus content declines.

soil-bio-125.title: Saprotrophs, the organisms that digest outside their bodies
soil-bio-125.text: A saprotroph never swallows its food. It feeds on dead organic matter or waste by secreting chemicals that digest it outside its body, unlike detritivores, which eat it. Fungi such as Mucor and soil bacteria do most of this work, and microscopic saprotrophs are also called saprobes. Their enzymes split proteins into amino acids, lipids into fatty acids and glycerol, starch into disaccharides and cellulose into glucose. Fungi take the products back into their hyphae and pass them through the mycelium for growth and repair. Saprotrophs need water, and fungi are 80–90% water. They also need oxygen, a neutral to mildly acidic pH below 7 and temperatures of 1 to 35 °C, growing best at 25 °C. Fungi decompose efficiently, which makes them among the main saprotrophs. Mycorrhizal fungi evolved from saprobic ancestors. Because saprotrophs recycle nutrients, the Royal Horticultural Society advises leaving them in gardens where possible.

soil-bio-107.title: How fallen leaves return nutrients to the soil
soil-bio-107.text: Before a leaf falls, the plant takes some of its nutrients back. Plants reabsorb part of their nutrients from aging leaves, and plants on poor sites reabsorb more, so their litter is nutrient-poor. What falls still feeds the soil. Litterfall nutrient cycling is the return of nutrients from plants to soil through fallen litter and its decomposition. It is the main pathway for recycling nitrogen and phosphorus. Organisms of decay turn the litter's simple carbon compounds into carbon dioxide and water. They release ions such as nitrogen and phosphorus, which plants take up again. Fungi play a large role. Rain and throughfall, the water dripping through the canopy, leach breakdown products into the soil. They add to its cation exchange capacity, especially in highly weathered tropical soils. Litter can also reshape a soil. Leaching of iron, aluminum and organic matter from litter drives podzolization. It is intense in boreal and cool temperate pine forests, whose litter is rich in phenolics and fulvic acid. Nutrient-rich litter decomposes faster. Nutrient levels measured by remote sensing therefore serve as an index of potential decomposition rate. An ecosystem's uptake equals the nutrients stored each year in plant tissues plus those replacing losses from litterfall and leaching.

soil-bio-126.title: The forest floor, between living trees and mineral soil
soil-bio-126.text: In tropical rainforests, termites and millipedes process litter so fast that the forest floor may vanish seasonally. Elsewhere it piles up. The forest floor, also called duff, is the layer of decaying litter and other dead plant matter between a forest's living vegetation and its mineral, humus-rich soil. In Canada and some other countries the term means the L, F and H layers: litter, visibly decomposing material and well-decomposed matter of unrecognizable origin. Specialists disagree on whether it equals the O horizon or leaves out the litter. Its mass reflects the balance of litter inputs and decay, set by site, vegetation and disturbance history. It is heaviest and deepest in boreal and mountain forests, where decay is slow. Its decomposition supplies a large share of a forest's nutrient needs. It is also an important fuel in forest fires. In one study of Douglas-fir seedlings, removing forest floor debris and compacting soil cut ectomycorrhizal fungal diversity and abundance by 60%.

soil-bio-095.title: Humus forms, the signature of how litter rots
soil-bio-095.text: Charles Darwin, a year before his death, published a detailed study of the crumbly surface soil he called mould. Today it is known as {{ref:soil-bio-096}}, one of several humus forms. A humus form is the group of organic and mineral-organic horizons at or near the surface that shows how litter becomes humus in a given place. It may include L, F, H and Ah horizons, but never B or C. Danish forester {{ref:soil-hist-012}} first described mull and its opposite, {{ref:soil-bio-104}}, linking them to the high and low fertility of beechwoods. Franz Hartmann later added {{ref:soil-bio-103}} between them. Five humus systems are now described on land: those three plus {{ref:soil-bio-097}} and {{ref:soil-bio-098}}. They occur from forests and grasslands to tundras and deserts. Soil organisms drive them, so humus profiles change within a few years, while whole soil profiles take decades to centuries. Foresters care because the humus form influences whether seedlings and saplings can establish and the forest can regenerate. Most humus classifications are national, such as the French, Belgian, German, Canadian and Russian ones, and focus on temperate forest soils. Bogs and marshes are classified differently. Their humus forms are sorted by the depth and seasonal swings of the water table and by dominant vegetation, such as sphagnum or herbs.

soil-bio-109.title: Raking the forest floor for animal bedding
soil-bio-109.text: In 1853 Europeans raked an estimated 50 Tg of dry leaf litter from their forests. That year was the peak of forest litter raking, an old practice widespread in Europe since the seventeenth century. Farmers gathered the litter to bed livestock in place of straw. Combined with other degradation, the raking could promote podzolization. Managed well, for example by burying the used litter, repeated removal may not harm soil formation. Primary forests hold more abundant, deeper and moister litter than secondary forests.

soil-bio-108.title: Litterbags, a simple tool for measuring decay
soil-bio-108.text: A mesh bag on the ground can measure a forest's metabolism. A litterbag is a container or mesh bag set out for a fixed time, either to collect falling litter or to measure how fast confined litter decays. Researchers place the bags at random, mark them by GPS or local coordinates and check them at set intervals. Weighing the dry contents gives the litterfall flux: total litter mass in kilograms divided by bag area in square meters, per year. Under a mass-balance approach, decomposition over a period should equal litterfall input over the same period. Different mesh sizes let researchers study different groups of soil animals.

soil-bio-111.title: Mangrove litter, where crabs do the cleanup
soil-bio-111.text: In some mangrove forests, crabs carry off 80% of the fallen leaves. Mangrove litterfall is litter that falls in mangrove forests or reaches coasts from rivers, and it follows a very different path from litter on land. Tides, crabs and microbes remove it, and which matters most depends on the tides. Where crabs dominate, they forage at low tide. Their droppings pass the leaves' tough woody compounds, undigested, into sediments and water. Each plant species' carbon can be traced from plant through crab to sediment.

soil-bio-132.title: Decomposers, the role that frees nutrients from the dead
soil-bio-132.text: A tree cannot hunt for its food. Plants and other sessile autotrophs, organisms that stay put and make their own food, cannot seek out nutrients or digest other organisms. They rely on decomposers, organisms that break down the dead and release the nutrients locked in dead matter. The word names a role, not a kind of organism. Fungi and bacteria fill it by digesting food outside their bodies. Earthworms and woodlice digest internally and release nutrients in their feces, so one organism can be both detritivore and decomposer. On land the work happens mainly in or on soil, and it makes soil more fertile. Earthworms and roots first grind and churn the material, a mixing called bioturbation. Enzymes do the rest. Enzymes for fats, proteins and starch are widespread, so these go first. Cellulases occur in far fewer organisms, and enzymes that digest {{ref:soil-bio-116}} in fewer still. Fungi are the primary litter decomposers in many ecosystems. Their hyphae penetrate large pieces that bacteria can only feed on from the surface, and only wood-decay fungi can modify that tough polymer.

soil-bio-110.title: Leaf litter as a home and a pantry
soil-bio-110.text: A layer of fallen leaves feeds and shelters a crowd. Its decomposer community includes fungi, bacteria, amoebae, nematodes, rotifers, tardigrades, springtails, potworms, insect larvae, mollusks, mites, woodlice and millipedes. Some plants are adapted to it. Bluebell shoots pierce the layer in spring, and rhizomatous wood sorrel thrives there. Salamanders and caecilians live in its damp microclimate, and the ovenbird needs it for foraging and nest material. In boreal forests, fallen lichens feed wintering deer and elk. In British Columbia they sustain mountain caribou through a 'manna effect'.

soil-bio-116.title: Lignin, the plant polymer that resists rot
soil-bio-116.text: Wood owes much of its strength to lignin. These complex polymers build the support tissues of plants, especially wood and bark. In cell walls it fills the spaces between cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin and cross-links them, so the plant stands firm and its vascular tissue can conduct water. Lignin resists decay and acid or base hydrolysis, and it shields cellulose from microbial enzymes. {{ref:soil-bio-129}} break it down with secreted peroxidases, and actinomycetes also decompose it. Under temperate conditions its half-life is about six months. Bound to proteins and microbial by-products, it becomes one of the main precursors of humus.
